case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Colorado's law prohibiting licensed mental health professionals from providing conversion therapy to minors violates the First Amendment's Free Speech Clause by restricting professional speech.
case_analysis.legal_provision: First Amendment Free Speech Clause (U.S. Constitution); Colorado's conversion therapy ban regulating licensed mental health professionals' conduct and speech with clients, enforced through the Colorado Department of Regulatory Agencies.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Kaley Chiles argues that Colorado's conversion therapy ban constitutes an unconstitutional restriction on protected speech, contending that talk therapy is fundamentally expressive speech rather than mere professional conduct, and that the government cannot selectively prohibit licensed counselors from engaging in certain viewpoints or therapeutic conversations with willing clients — particularly where the restriction is content- and viewpoint-based, targeting specific therapeutic messages rather than regulating conduct incidentally burdening speech.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Colorado officials argue that the conversion therapy ban is a permissible regulation of professional conduct that only incidentally burdens speech, asserting that states have broad authority to regulate the practice of licensed professions to protect client welfare — particularly minors — and that such regulations need only satisfy rational basis or intermediate scrutiny rather than strict scrutiny, as the law targets harmful therapeutic practices rather than suppressing a viewpoint in the broader public marketplace of ideas.
key_precedents: NIFLA v. Becerra, 585 U.S. 755 (2018) — rejecting a separate category of 'professional speech' entitled to reduced First Amendment protection
Planned Parenthood v. Casey, 505 U.S. 833 (1992) — recognizing state authority to regulate the medical profession
Reed v. Town of Gilbert, 576 U.S. 155 (2015) — establishing strict scrutiny for content-based speech restrictions
United States v. Stevens, 559 U.S. 460 (2010) — rejecting ad hoc balancing tests for new categories of unprotected speech
Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project, 561 U.S. 1 (2010) — addressing speech restrictions in the context of professional and instructional communications
Otto v. City of Boca Raton, 981 F.3d 854 (11th Cir. 2020) — striking down conversion therapy bans as unconstitutional speech restrictions
Pickup v. Brown, 740 F.3d 1208 (9th Cir. 2014) — upholding conversion therapy bans as regulations of professional conduct
Tingley v. Ferguson, 47 F.4th 1055 (9th Cir. 2022) — upholding Washington State's conversion therapy ban under NIFLA framework
Lowe v. SEC, 472 U.S. 181 (1985) — discussing limits of professional regulation on speech
Sorrell v. IMS Health Inc., 564 U.S. 552 (2011) — applying heightened scrutiny to content- and speaker-based speech restrictions

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan's argument that the viewpoint asymmetry in Colorado's law merely tracks an evidence-based standard of care — analogizing to prohibitions on thalidomide prescriptions — remains the most serious challenge to my position, but the analogy ultimately fails because thalidomide is a physical substance whose prohibition has no operative effect on communicative content, whereas Colorado's law has no operative effect on anything except the words spoken and the viewpoint they convey. Justice Kavanaugh's workability concern continues to be the argument that most moves me institutionally, and it is precisely why I would write the narrowest possible majority opinion: holding only that verbal talk therapy constitutes speech subject to heightened scrutiny and remanding for lower courts to apply that standard, explicitly reserving questions about physical therapeutic modalities, informed consent requirements, and other professional regulations. This narrow remand approach — which I believe could attract Justice Kavanaugh and potentially Justice Kagan — would avoid the destabilizing consequences both raise while still vindicating the core principle that viewpoint-discriminatory restrictions on communicative content cannot be laundered through the licensing power. As Chief Justice, my obligation to institutional legitimacy counsels writing the smallest opinion that resolves this case, not the broadest one that forecloses every adjacent question Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor rightly identify as consequential.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan make the most serious opposing argument — that Colorado is regulating professional conduct within a fiduciary relationship rather than suppressing viewpoints in the public marketplace, and that NIFLA itself acknowledged Casey's principle permitting conduct regulation that incidentally burdens speech. But this argument fails under my originalist methodology and under NIFLA's own logic: the original public meaning of the First Amendment protected speech from government censorship of particular messages, and there is no historical tradition at the Founding of licensing regimes being deployed to prohibit specific viewpoints communicated between consenting adults and their chosen counselors. The conduct/speech distinction my colleagues invoke collapses here because Colorado's law has no operative effect on any physical act — the only thing being regulated is the communicative content of words spoken, selected precisely because of their viewpoint, which is the paradigmatic case NIFLA addressed when it rejected the professional speech doctrine. Justice Kavanaugh's suggestion of rational basis or intermediate scrutiny finds no support in the original public meaning of the First Amendment or in NIFLA's text, which did not carve out a licensed-professional exception to content-based scrutiny but instead reaffirmed that Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project applied strict scrutiny to professional speech regulations.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson's invocation of historical quack medicine laws as evidence of broad state police power over licensed healing professions is the most novel argument raised in this round, but it fails under careful examination: those historical regulations targeted fraudulent factual claims and physically dangerous procedures, not the suppression of one therapeutic viewpoint while permitting the opposite — the asymmetry that makes Colorado's law viewpoint-discriminatory rather than merely a professional conduct standard. Justice Kavanaugh's workability concern remains the most serious challenge to my position, but as Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies, the answer is a clear limiting principle — strict scrutiny applies when the law's operative restriction targets communicative content rather than a separable physical act — not an unprincipled exception that would allow states to launder viewpoint discrimination through occupational licensing simply by calling it 'practice regulation.' Justice Kagan's intermediate scrutiny proposal finds no textual or doctrinal anchor in NIFLA, which did not create a licensed-professional-relationship exception to content-based scrutiny but instead reaffirmed that Holder's strict scrutiny framework governs professional speech regulations. Colorado has not demonstrated that less restrictive alternatives — informed consent requirements, mandatory disclosure of scientific consensus, parental consent protocols — were inadequate, and that failure is fatal regardless of whether we characterize the state's interest as parens patriae or public health.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett's viewpoint discrimination argument remains the most formidable challenge, and I want to engage it with full seriousness: she is correct that Colorado's law creates an asymmetry — affirmation is permitted, change-oriented therapy is not — but this asymmetry is constitutionally indistinguishable from a state prohibiting a licensed physician from prescribing a drug the medical consensus deems harmful while permitting alternative treatments. The asymmetry tracks evidence, not viewpoint suppression. Justice Gorsuch's limiting principle — strict scrutiny when the law targets communicative content rather than a separable physical act — is the strongest version of the petitioner argument, but it proves too much: recovered memory therapy bans, prohibitions on fraudulent diagnosis, and malpractice standards all operate through restricting communicative content, and subjecting all such regulations to strict scrutiny would, as Justice Jackson correctly warns, unsettle the entire architecture of evidence-based professional licensing in ways no prior Court has sanctioned. Chief Justice Roberts' narrow remand approach is institutionally attractive, but remanding for lower courts to apply strict scrutiny to verbal talk therapy effectively decides the constitutional question against Colorado while deferring the formal holding — I would rather write a clear dissent establishing that intermediate scrutiny governs licensed fiduciary relationships with minors who cannot meaningfully consent, a standard Colorado's law survives given the documented psychological harm and the state's parens patriae authority at its apex.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett's viewpoint asymmetry argument remains the most formidable challenge to my position, and I want to be precise about why it ultimately does not compel strict scrutiny here: the asymmetry she identifies — permitting affirmation while prohibiting the opposite message — tracks the evidentiary record of harm, not the state's preference for one viewpoint over another in public discourse. A state that prohibits a licensed oncologist from recommending Laetrile while permitting evidence-based chemotherapy is not engaging in viewpoint discrimination; it is enforcing a standard of care, and the fact that the standard happens to align with one therapeutic direction does not transform the regulation into viewpoint suppression. Chief Justice Roberts' narrow remand proposal is genuinely attractive to me institutionally — it would avoid the destabilizing consequences Justice Jackson correctly identifies while still engaging the First Amendment question — but I worry that remanding for 'heightened scrutiny' without specifying the standard effectively hands lower courts a blank check to invalidate the entire architecture of evidence-based professional licensing, which is precisely the unworkable outcome Justice Kavanaugh and I have been warning against. I maintain that intermediate scrutiny is the appropriate standard within a licensed fiduciary relationship with a minor, and Colorado's law survives that standard given the documented psychological harm and the absence of credible scientific support for the practice.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh make the most serious opposing argument — that NIFLA itself preserved Casey's principle that states may regulate professional conduct even when speech is incidentally burdened, and that Colorado's law targets a therapeutic practice rather than suppressing viewpoints in public discourse. But this argument proves too much and elides the critical distinction NIFLA drew: the Casey carve-out applies to regulations of professional conduct that incidentally burden speech, not to laws whose operative mechanism is the prohibition of specific communicative content selected precisely because of its viewpoint. Colorado's law does not prohibit a physical act, a procedure, or a non-expressive practice — it prohibits words, specifically words conveying a particular therapeutic message, while permitting counselors to convey the opposite message freely. That is the definition of viewpoint discrimination, and the fact that it occurs within a licensed professional relationship cannot launder it into permissible conduct regulation any more than a state could prohibit licensed attorneys from advising clients to assert their Fifth Amendment rights on the theory that legal advice is 'professional conduct.' Justice Kavanaugh's workability concern about destabilizing professional regulation is real, but the answer is a clear rule — strict scrutiny applies when the law's operative restriction targets communicative content rather than a separable physical act — not abandoning First Amendment protection for all speech that occurs within a licensed professional relationship.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts' narrow remand proposal is the argument that most moves me this round — holding only that verbal talk therapy constitutes speech subject to heightened scrutiny and remanding, while explicitly reserving questions about physical therapeutic modalities and informed consent requirements, is precisely the kind of institutionally cautious, minimalist approach I find attractive. However, I cannot join that holding because it still accepts the premise that strict scrutiny applies, and I remain unpersuaded that NIFLA silently eliminated Casey's conduct-regulation carve-out in the licensed-professional context. Justice Barrett's viewpoint asymmetry argument is powerful, but the thalidomide analogy Justice Kagan offers captures my intuition: a state may prohibit a licensed physician from recommending a treatment the medical community has identified as harmful to a vulnerable patient who cannot meaningfully consent, and that asymmetric prohibition reflects a professional standard of care rather than viewpoint discrimination, even when the prohibited 'treatment' is delivered through words. I would apply intermediate scrutiny — Colorado's law survives that standard given the documented psychological harm to minors and the absence of scientific consensus supporting the practice — and I write separately to emphasize that this holding is narrow and does not disturb the broader architecture of evidence-based professional licensing.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Kagan raise the most serious challenge to my position — that NIFLA itself preserved Casey's principle that states may regulate professional conduct even when speech is incidentally burdened, and that Colorado is merely conditioning a license on adherence to standards of care rather than suppressing viewpoints in the public marketplace. But this argument proves too much and elides the critical distinction NIFLA drew: the law here does not regulate a physical therapeutic modality that incidentally involves words, but rather regulates the words themselves, selected precisely because of their communicative content and viewpoint. A counselor who says 'your same-sex attraction can change' violates the law; one who says 'your same-sex attraction is immutable and healthy' does not — this is paradigmatic viewpoint discrimination that cannot be laundered through the licensing power, as NIFLA's rejection of a professional speech carve-out makes clear. Justice Kavanaugh's 'workability' concern about destabilizing professional regulation is legitimate but ultimately unpersuasive under my textualist methodology, because the answer to administrability concerns cannot be to create an unprincipled exception that swallows the First Amendment's core prohibition on viewpoint discrimination — the proper limiting principle is that states may regulate conduct with incidental speech effects, but not regulate speech itself under the guise of conduct regulation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett's viewpoint discrimination argument remains the most formidable challenge, and I want to engage it with full seriousness: she is correct that the law permits one therapeutic message while prohibiting the other, and under Reed v. Town of Gilbert that asymmetry would ordinarily trigger strict scrutiny. But I continue to believe this framing fundamentally mischaracterizes the constitutional posture because it treats all communicative acts within a licensed fiduciary relationship as equivalent to speech in the public marketplace — a position NIFLA itself did not fully embrace, as Justice Kagan correctly notes in preserving Casey's conduct-regulation principle. The thalidomide analogy I find most persuasive: a state may prohibit a licensed physician from prescribing a treatment the medical community has identified as harmful to a vulnerable patient population, and that prohibition is viewpoint-asymmetric in precisely the same way Barrett identifies — yet no one seriously argues it triggers strict scrutiny, because the asymmetry tracks an evidence-based standard of care rather than government hostility to a disfavored message. Justice Gorsuch's limiting principle — strict scrutiny when the law targets communicative content rather than a separable physical act — is cleaner than my position, but as Justice Kavanaugh correctly observes, it proves too much by subjecting prohibitions on recovered memory therapy, fraudulent diagnosis, and unproven medical advice to strict scrutiny, which would unsettle the entire architecture of evidence-based professional licensing in ways that the First Amendment's original purpose of protecting political discourse from government censorship simply does not require.

John Roberts.reasoning: NIFLA v. Becerra (2018) explicitly rejected the notion of a separate 'professional speech' doctrine entitled to reduced First Amendment protection, which forecloses Colorado's primary argument that talk therapy by licensed professionals occupies a diminished constitutional category. The Colorado law is content-based on its face — it prohibits specific therapeutic messages and viewpoints directed at a particular outcome — which under Reed v. Town of Gilbert presumptively triggers strict scrutiny that the state cannot satisfy merely by invoking its licensing authority. While I am deeply sympathetic to Colorado's interest in protecting minors from potentially harmful practices, and while I would prefer to resolve this on the narrowest possible grounds, the post-NIFLA framework does not permit states to evade First Amendment scrutiny simply by characterizing regulated speech as 'professional conduct' when the law's operative restriction targets the content and viewpoint of the communication itself rather than a separable physical act. I would hold narrowly that Colorado's ban as applied to licensed counselors' verbal therapeutic sessions constitutes a content-based speech restriction subject to heightened scrutiny, while leaving open questions about the precise standard and remanding for further proceedings, thereby avoiding a sweeping ruling on professional regulation generally.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Colorado's conversion therapy ban is a content-based and viewpoint-based restriction on speech that targets specific therapeutic messages rather than regulating conduct that merely incidentally involves speech — the law does not prohibit the physical acts of therapy but rather the specific verbal content and viewpoint expressed during sessions. Under NIFLA v. Becerra, this Court explicitly rejected a separate 'professional speech' doctrine that would subject professional communications to reduced First Amendment scrutiny, and under Reed v. Town of Gilbert, content-based speech restrictions presumptively trigger strict scrutiny regardless of the professional context in which they arise. The original public meaning of the First Amendment, as understood at the Founding, protected the freedom of speech and press from government censorship of particular messages and viewpoints, and there is no historical tradition of licensing regimes being used to suppress specific viewpoints communicated between consenting adults and their chosen counselors. Colorado cannot satisfy strict scrutiny here, as the government's interest, however characterized, does not justify a viewpoint-discriminatory prohibition on what licensed professionals may say to willing minor clients and their families who seek this form of counseling.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under NIFLA v. Becerra, there is no separate 'professional speech' doctrine affording reduced First Amendment protection, and Colorado's conversion therapy ban targets the communicative content of therapeutic speech itself — not conduct that incidentally burdens speech. The law is plainly content- and viewpoint-based under Reed v. Town of Gilbert, prohibiting specific therapeutic messages while permitting counselors to convey the opposite viewpoint, which triggers strict scrutiny that Colorado cannot satisfy by merely labeling talk therapy as 'conduct.' While I am generally skeptical of expansive First Amendment claims that hamper regulatory authority, the text and logic of NIFLA compel the conclusion that when the State's only target is the words a licensed professional speaks — selected precisely because of their communicative content — the incidental-burden exception does not apply, and the government must satisfy strict scrutiny. Colorado has not demonstrated that a content-neutral or less speech-restrictive alternative was unavailable to protect minors from harmful therapeutic practices.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: While NIFLA v. Becerra (2018) correctly rejected a categorical 'professional speech' doctrine entitled to reduced scrutiny, Colorado's conversion therapy ban is best understood as a regulation of professional conduct — the practice of a licensed therapeutic modality — that only incidentally burdens speech, analogous to the state's broad authority recognized in Planned Parenthood v. Casey to regulate medical and mental health professions to protect patient welfare. The critical distinction is that Colorado is not suppressing a viewpoint in the public marketplace of ideas but rather regulating what licensed professionals may do within a fiduciary therapeutic relationship with vulnerable minor clients, where the state's parens patriae interest is at its apex and the scientific consensus documents serious psychological harm. Even accepting that heightened scrutiny applies under NIFLA's framework, Colorado's compelling interest in protecting minors from demonstrably harmful pseudoscientific practices — backed by consensus from the APA, AMA, and AAP — is sufficiently weighty, and the restriction is narrowly tailored to the licensed professional-minor client context rather than reaching public advocacy or private speech. The Ninth Circuit's reasoning in Tingley v. Ferguson (2022) is more persuasive than the Eleventh Circuit's Otto approach because it properly accounts for the state's legitimate regulatory authority over licensed conduct within the therapeutic relationship without immunizing all professional speech from First Amendment scrutiny.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: While NIFLA correctly rejected a categorical 'professional speech' doctrine and I take seriously the concern that Colorado is restricting speech based on its communicative content, the more workable and textually coherent framework recognizes that states retain meaningful authority to regulate licensed professional practice to protect vulnerable clients — particularly minors — from treatments the state has determined to be harmful and lacking scientific support. The critical distinction from NIFLA is that Colorado is not compelling speech or mandating a viewpoint in the public marketplace; it is licensing a profession and conditioning that license on adherence to standards of care, which is precisely the kind of conduct regulation Planned Parenthood v. Casey and the NIFLA majority itself acknowledged as permissible when it noted states may regulate professional conduct even where speech is incidentally burdened. I am persuaded that the Tingley v. Ferguson framework better captures the practical reality here: the law targets a therapeutic practice within a fiduciary, client-professional relationship rather than suppressing a viewpoint in broader public discourse, and applying strict scrutiny to every professional licensing standard that touches on communicative content would dangerously unsettle the entire edifice of professional regulation. That said, I would write narrowly to preserve strict scrutiny for regulations that are genuinely viewpoint-discriminatory in the public sphere, consistent with Reed v. Town of Gilbert, while affirming Colorado's authority in this specific licensed-practice context.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under NIFLA v. Becerra, this Court expressly rejected the notion that 'professional speech' constitutes a separate category entitled to diminished First Amendment protection, and Colorado cannot circumvent that holding by relabeling talk therapy as 'conduct' when the only thing being regulated is the communicative content of a licensed counselor's words. As Reed v. Town of Gilbert makes clear, content-based restrictions on speech — and this law is plainly content-based, targeting specific therapeutic messages because of their viewpoint — trigger strict scrutiny, which Colorado's ban cannot survive absent a compelling interest pursued through narrowly tailored means. The government's power to license a profession does not grant it unfettered authority to dictate which ideas a licensed professional may express to a willing client; as Sorrell v. IMS Health recognized, speaker- and content-based burdens on speech demand heightened judicial scrutiny regardless of the professional context. Applying the rule that the government cannot launder viewpoint discrimination through occupational licensing regimes, and consistent with the Eleventh Circuit's reasoning in Otto v. City of Boca Raton, I would hold that Colorado's conversion therapy ban as applied to the speech of licensed mental health professionals violates the First Amendment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Colorado's conversion therapy ban is best understood as a regulation of professional conduct within the licensed therapist-client relationship that incidentally burdens speech, consistent with NIFLA v. Becerra's recognition that states retain authority to regulate professional conduct even when that conduct involves verbal communication. NIFLA explicitly reaffirmed Casey's principle that communications 'as part of the practice of' a licensed profession can be regulated as professional conduct, and Colorado's law targets a specific therapeutic practice performed by licensed professionals rather than suppressing viewpoints in the broader public marketplace of ideas — a counselor remains free to discuss, advocate for, or write about conversion therapy outside the clinical relationship. History and tradition support broad state police power to regulate licensed professions to protect vulnerable populations, particularly minors, from practices the state's legislature has determined to be harmful, and the practical workability concerns of subjecting every professional licensing regulation to strict scrutiny would be substantial and destabilizing. While I take seriously the Eleventh Circuit's concerns in Otto about viewpoint discrimination, the more institutionally restrained course is to recognize that the professional-client therapeutic context is meaningfully distinct from general public discourse, and rational basis or at most intermediate scrutiny should govern here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under NIFLA v. Becerra, there is no separate category of 'professional speech' entitled to reduced First Amendment protection, and Colorado's conversion therapy ban is a content-based restriction on speech that must survive strict scrutiny under Reed v. Town of Gilbert. The law targets specific therapeutic messages and viewpoints — not merely professional conduct — because the 'conduct' being regulated is speech itself, regulated precisely because of disapproval of its expressive content; a licensing requirement cannot strip speech of its First Amendment protection simply by categorizing it as professional conduct. As NIFLA explicitly recognized, Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project applied strict scrutiny to content-based laws regulating professional speech, and Colorado's law cannot escape that rigorous standard by characterizing talk therapy as mere conduct when the restriction operates directly on communicative content between a willing counselor and willing client. While states retain legitimate authority to regulate professional conduct under Planned Parenthood v. Casey, that authority does not extend to viewpoint-discriminatory suppression of therapeutic conversations that are fundamentally expressive in nature, and Colorado has not demonstrated the compelling interest and narrow tailoring that strict scrutiny demands.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: While NIFLA v. Becerra (2018) correctly rejected a freestanding 'professional speech' doctrine immune from First Amendment scrutiny, Colorado's conversion therapy ban is best understood as a regulation of professional conduct — the practice of a licensed therapeutic modality — that incidentally burdens speech, rather than a viewpoint-based suppression of ideas in the public marketplace. The State's compelling interest in protecting minors from documented psychological harm caused by conversion therapy practices, combined with its broad authority under Planned Parenthood v. Casey to regulate licensed medical and mental health professions, supports applying intermediate rather than strict scrutiny here. Unlike the compelled disclosure at issue in NIFLA, Colorado is not forcing practitioners to convey a government-approved message but is instead restricting a specific harmful practice within a licensed, regulated professional relationship with a uniquely vulnerable population — minors who cannot meaningfully consent. The circuit split between Otto v. City of Boca Raton and Tingley v. Ferguson reflects genuine doctrinal tension, but the weight of the state's interest in child welfare and the practical consequences of invalidating evidence-based professional regulations tips the balance toward upholding the law under intermediate scrutiny.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Colorado's law prohibiting licensed mental health professionals from providing 'conversion therapy' to minors violates the First Amendment's Free Speech Clause by restricting professional speech during client consultations.
case_analysis.legal_provision: First Amendment Free Speech Clause (U.S. Constitution); Colorado's conversion therapy prohibition statute regulating the practice of licensed mental health professionals (enforced through the Colorado Department of Regulatory Agencies)
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Kaley Chiles argues that Colorado's ban on conversion therapy constitutes an unconstitutional restriction on protected speech, contending that verbal communications between a licensed therapist and a client are First Amendment-protected expression that cannot be categorically suppressed by the government simply by labeling it 'professional conduct,' and that the law imposes a viewpoint- or content-based restriction on therapeutic speech without surviving appropriate constitutional scrutiny.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Colorado state officials argue that the conversion therapy prohibition is a legitimate regulation of professional conduct rather than a restriction on protected speech, asserting that states have broad authority to regulate the practice of licensed professions — including the methods and techniques professionals may employ — and that any incidental burden on speech is permissible under rational basis or intermediate scrutiny as a valid exercise of the state's police power to protect the health and welfare of minors.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan's continued insistence that the Casey carve-out survives NIFLA for conduct-within-licensing-regime regulations remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I credit her pragmatic concern that a remand without a clearer limiting principle risks constitutionalizing malpractice standards and informed-consent requirements — Justice Jackson makes this point with particular force. However, the limiting principle I would articulate in the majority opinion is precisely the one NIFLA provides: the Casey carve-out applies where speech is genuinely incidental to separately regulated non-expressive conduct, and Colorado's law has no such non-expressive anchor — its entire operative effect is to prohibit verbal communications based on their content and therapeutic orientation, which is the paradigm NIFLA identified as requiring heightened scrutiny. I am writing narrowly: heightened scrutiny applies, we do not specify strict scrutiny categorically, and we remand for the lower courts to apply that standard with a full evidentiary record — this preserves Colorado's ability to regulate if it can satisfy the standard, addresses Justice Sotomayor's legitimate concern about the documented harm to minors (which goes to whether scrutiny is satisfied, not whether it applies), and provides circuit-split clarity without the categorical overreach Justice Thomas would prefer. As Chief Justice, I would assign this opinion to myself precisely because the institutional stakes of getting the limiting principle right are high enough that I want to control the narrowness of the holding.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the most sophisticated argument for the Respondent — that Colorado's law regulates professional conduct (methods and techniques) rather than speech as such, and that NIFLA preserved this distinction. But this argument cannot survive scrutiny when applied to the facts here: Colorado's law does not prohibit a physical technique, a drug, or a non-verbal intervention — it prohibits therapists from engaging in verbal communications that express or facilitate a particular viewpoint about sexual orientation change. The 'incidental burden' carve-out NIFLA preserved applies to regulations where speech is genuinely incidental to separately regulated non-expressive conduct, as in Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project where the material support prohibition targeted coordination with terrorist organizations, not the ideas expressed. Here, the speech IS the conduct — there is no non-expressive therapeutic technique being regulated; the law's entire operative effect is to prohibit certain words, arguments, and therapeutic orientations based on their content and viewpoint. Justice Alito's concern about constitutionalizing all professional verbal exchanges is legitimate, but the limiting principle is precisely what NIFLA provides: regulations that genuinely target non-expressive conduct with incidental speech effects survive, while those that target communicative content based on viewpoint — as Colorado's law plainly does by permitting affirmation while prohibiting change-oriented speech — must satisfy strict scrutiny, which the State has not demonstrated it can meet.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that NIFLA explicitly rejected the Ninth Circuit's Pickup reasoning remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I acknowledge it has genuine force — but I continue to believe it overstates NIFLA's reach. The Casey carve-out NIFLA preserved was not merely a categorical escape hatch; it reflected a substantive judgment that some professional-client verbal exchanges are better understood as regulated conduct than as speech in the constitutional sense, and the question of which standard applies to that preserved category remains genuinely open. Justice Thomas's 'the speech IS the conduct' argument proves too much, as Justice Jackson correctly identifies — by that logic, prohibitions on fraudulent medical advice, informed-consent mandates, and malpractice standards governing physician communications would all require strict scrutiny, constitutionalizing the entire edifice of professional licensing in ways no NIFLA majority member contemplated. I remain with the Respondent position because the conduct-speech line must be drawn somewhere, and a clinical technique deployed within a licensed therapeutic relationship on a minor who cannot meaningfully consent sits closer to the conduct pole — though I acknowledge this is a close case and Chief Justice Roberts' remand approach has genuine institutional appeal as a way to avoid the binary choice.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that NIFLA forecloses the conduct-regulation framing is the strongest opposing argument, but it misreads what NIFLA actually preserved. NIFLA rejected a categorical 'professional speech' doctrine that would automatically reduce scrutiny, but it explicitly preserved — citing Planned Parenthood v. Casey — the principle that 'regulations of professional conduct that incidentally involve speech' are not subject to heightened scrutiny. Colorado's law regulates the methods and techniques of licensed clinical practice, not the therapist's right to hold or express views in public discourse; a therapist remains free to write, speak, and advocate for conversion therapy outside the clinical relationship. Justice Gorsuch's textualist argument that 'speech is not unprotected merely because it is uttered by professionals' proves too much — it would constitutionalize every malpractice standard, every informed-consent requirement, every prohibition on fraudulent medical advice, all of which involve verbal communications between licensed professionals and clients. The documented, severe psychological harm to LGBTQ+ minors — increased suicidality, depression, and trauma — combined with the near-universal condemnation of conversion therapy by major medical and psychological associations, provides Colorado with a more than sufficient evidentiary basis to sustain this regulation under any scrutiny below strict, and the state's interest in protecting children who cannot meaningfully consent to these interventions is precisely the kind of compelling welfare interest that justifies professional licensing restrictions.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument remains the most serious challenge to my position, and I want to engage it with full candor: she is correct that NIFLA rejected Pickup's conduct-within-licensing-regime framing, but I read that rejection as targeting the categorical version of that doctrine — the automatic reduction in scrutiny for any professional speech — rather than eliminating the fact-specific Casey inquiry into whether a particular regulation targets communicative content as such or regulates a clinical technique whose implementation requires words. The word 'incidentally' that Justice Barrett emphasizes actually supports my reading: in Colorado's law, the verbal exchange is incidental to the therapeutic relationship being regulated, just as in Casey the speech was incidental to the abortion procedure, whereas in NIFLA the compelled disclosure was the entire operative mechanism with no separable non-expressive conduct. Justice Thomas's 'speech IS the conduct' argument, which Justice Barrett implicitly endorses, proves too much — as Justice Jackson correctly identifies, it would require strict scrutiny for every malpractice standard, every prohibition on fraudulent medical advice, and every informed-consent requirement, none of which the NIFLA majority contemplated immunizing from state regulation. I remain persuaded that Chief Justice Roberts' remand approach, while institutionally attractive, requires a limiting principle that the petitioner's side has not supplied, and without that principle I cannot join a ruling that would constitutionalize the entire edifice of professional licensing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the most sophisticated version of the respondent's argument — that NIFLA preserved the Casey principle for 'regulations of professional conduct that incidentally involve speech,' and that Colorado's law targets a clinical technique within a licensing regime rather than suppressing viewpoint in public discourse. But this argument cannot survive the precise distinction NIFLA drew: the Court there explicitly rejected the Ninth Circuit's Pickup reasoning, which employed exactly this conduct-within-licensing-regime framing, meaning the respondents are asking us to resurrect the very analytical move NIFLA interred. Justice Sotomayor's invocation of documented harms to minors is genuinely weighty, but as Justice Barrett correctly notes, severity of harm goes to whether strict scrutiny is satisfied — not to whether it applies — and Colorado has not demonstrated that a categorical ban rather than more tailored regulations constitutes the least restrictive means. I am persuaded by Chief Justice Roberts' instinct that the narrowest path is remanding for proper scrutiny analysis rather than categorical invalidation, which addresses Justice Jackson's legitimate concern about unraveling professional licensing regimes while faithfully applying NIFLA's holding that content-based professional speech restrictions require heightened scrutiny.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson's argument that NIFLA only rejected a categorical professional speech doctrine — not the Casey carve-out for conduct regulations that incidentally involve speech — is the most sophisticated remaining challenge, and I take it seriously. But the 'incidentally' qualifier is doing critical work that Justice Jackson's framing elides: in Casey, the informed-consent requirement regulated a separately identifiable non-expressive act (performing an abortion), with speech genuinely incidental to that conduct; Colorado's law has no such separable non-expressive predicate — its entire operative effect is to prohibit certain verbal communications based on their content and therapeutic orientation. Justice Sotomayor's concern about constitutionalizing malpractice standards and informed-consent requirements is legitimate, but the limiting principle is precisely what NIFLA provides: those regulations target non-expressive conduct (performing a procedure, prescribing a drug) with speech incidentally attached, whereas Colorado's law targets the speech itself as the regulated 'conduct,' which is the paradigm case NIFLA identified as requiring heightened scrutiny. I continue to favor Chief Justice Roberts' narrowest path — applying heightened scrutiny and remanding for a proper evidentiary record rather than categorical invalidation — which preserves states' regulatory authority if they can satisfy the standard while remaining faithful to NIFLA's core holding.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Jackson's argument that NIFLA only rejected a categorical professional speech doctrine — not the fact-specific Casey carve-out — remains the most sophisticated challenge to my position, and I want to engage it with full seriousness: the distinction she draws between categorical escape hatches and fact-specific inquiries is real, but it cannot save Colorado's law because the fact-specific inquiry NIFLA preserved asks whether speech is *incidental* to separately regulated non-expressive conduct, and here there is no non-expressive conduct — the law's entire operative mechanism is prohibiting verbal communications based on their therapeutic orientation and content. Justice Alito's surgeon hypothetical is genuinely illuminating but ultimately distinguishable: a prohibition on a surgeon verbally walking a patient through dangerous self-surgery regulates the non-expressive act of surgery and the verbal instruction is incidental to that separately prohibited conduct, whereas Colorado's law has no non-expressive referent — it targets the words and their meaning directly. My background as a public defender reinforces my conviction that when the doctrinal path leads to immunizing documented psychological harm to vulnerable minors from state regulation simply because the harm is inflicted through words in a coercive clinical relationship, we have followed the logic somewhere the First Amendment was never designed to go.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under NIFLA v. Becerra, this Court expressly rejected a separate 'professional speech' doctrine that would categorically subject licensed professionals' speech to reduced First Amendment scrutiny, and Colorado's law cannot escape that holding simply by labeling talk therapy as 'conduct' when the only thing being regulated is the verbal content of therapeutic communications. Becerra (2018) expressly rejected a separate 'professional speech' doctrine and made clear that content-based regulations of professional speech are subject to the same First Amendment scrutiny as other content-based restrictions — the government cannot escape rigorous scrutiny by labeling targeted speech as 'professional conduct.' The verbal communications between a licensed therapist and a minor client are quintessentially speech, and Colorado's law discriminates based on the content and viewpoint of that speech by permitting therapists to affirm certain conclusions about sexual orientation while prohibiting others, which under Reed v. Town of Gilbert triggers strict scrutiny that Colorado cannot satisfy. The circuit split is real and the question is close, but the state's interest in protecting minors' welfare through professional licensing regulation, applied to conduct-focused restrictions rather than viewpoint suppression of public discourse, tips the balance toward upholding the statute under intermediate scrutiny.

As NIFLA v. Becerra itself acknowledged, regulations of professional conduct that incidentally burden speech do not automatically require strict or intermediate scrutiny, and the state's broad police power to protect the health and welfare of minors through professional licensing regimes is well-established under Barsky and its progeny. The real-world harm to LGBTQ+ youth subjected to conversion therapy — including documented increases in depression, suicidality, and psychological trauma — weighs heavily in my analysis, as the First Amendment was never intended to shield licensed professionals from accountability when their 'speech' constitutes a harmful clinical intervention on vulnerable minors who cannot meaningfully consent. Petitioner's framing would dangerously unravel countless professional licensing regimes by constitutionalizing any verbal exchange between a licensed provider and client, a result neither NIFLA nor Reed v. Town of Gilbert compels.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: While NIFLA correctly rejected a freestanding 'professional speech' doctrine that would automatically reduce scrutiny for any regulation touching licensed professionals, it did not eliminate the distinction between regulations that target speech as such and those that regulate professional conduct with incidental effects on communication. Colorado's conversion therapy ban is best understood as regulating the methods and techniques of licensed mental health practice — the therapeutic relationship itself — rather than suppressing a viewpoint in the broader public discourse, and states have historically exercised broad police power to define the standard of care within licensed professions. The critical textual and structural question is whether the law regulates what a professional does in a clinical setting or what a professional may say generally, and here the restriction is tethered to the licensing regime, applies only within the professional-client relationship, and serves the state's compelling interest in protecting minors from documented psychological harm — a workable limiting principle that avoids the slippery slope of immunizing all professional conduct from regulation simply because it involves words. That said, I would require the state to demonstrate more than rational basis given NIFLA's warning against reflexive deference, and would look to intermediate scrutiny as the appropriate standard, which Colorado's evidence-based justifications appear to satisfy.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Colorado's conversion therapy prohibition, as applied to licensed mental health professionals engaged in verbal consultations with minor clients, constitutes a content-based restriction on speech that must survive strict scrutiny under NIFLA v. Becerra, which expressly rejected the existence of a separate 'professional speech' doctrine permitting reduced scrutiny for content-based regulations simply because the speaker holds a license. The plain text of the First Amendment protects speech, and the government cannot launder a speech restriction into a mere 'conduct regulation' by affixing the label of professional practice to what is, at its core, the regulation of what a therapist may say to a client during a consultation — as NIFLA made clear, 'speech is not unprotected merely because it is uttered by professionals.' Town of Gilbert confirms that content-based restrictions — those that target speech based on its communicative content or viewpoint — are presumptively unconstitutional, and Colorado's law plainly targets speech advocating or facilitating a particular therapeutic orientation regarding sexual orientation, which is quintessentially content- and viewpoint-based. While states retain genuine authority to regulate professional conduct, including licensing standards and non-expressive techniques, that authority does not extend to dictating the substantive content of professional advice and counsel, and the rule of lenity in construing restrictions on constitutional liberties counsels against permitting such a broad regulatory carve-out to swallow First Amendment protections.

Town of Gilbert triggers heightened scrutiny that the state's interest, however legitimate, must survive. My institutionalist instincts counsel caution about broadly invalidating state regulatory schemes, but NIFLA's reasoning forecloses the conduct-regulation escape hatch Colorado relies upon, and I cannot sustain a content-based speech restriction that fails to survive the scrutiny our precedents demand.

I write with some hesitation given the genuine state interest at stake and the possibility that a more developed factual record on harm could alter the strict scrutiny calculus, but methodological consistency with NIFLA compels this result.

Becerra (2018) reaffirmed, states retain broad authority to regulate the practice of licensed professions, including methods employed during client consultations, and the Court explicitly preserved the principle from Casey that verbal communications 'as part of the practice of' a licensed profession may be regulated as professional conduct.
